extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, dramatists and creative writers studying Aristotle's Poetics and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and analysing dramatic poetry (tragedy and comedy), focusing on the relations of plot and character, universalisation/idealisation, comic/ludicrous effects, and naming/typification in plays. Draws on Aristotle's Poetics as interpreted in a literary textbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot is the first artistic necessity of drama
rubrics_metrics.description: For the drama, in its true idea, is a poetical representation of a complete and typical action, whose lines converge on a determined end; which evolves itself out of human emotion and human will in such a manner that action and character are each in turn the outcome of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a unified action with a beginning, middle, and end; build the plot so its events converge on a determined end and both drive and reflect character. Avoid loose or episodic sequences that lack moral or causal cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the gradual evolution of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern drama delights in being present at the determining moment of a man's career, to watch the dawning of a passion, the shaping of a purpose, and to pursue the deed to its final accomplishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict each step in a character's process of becoming — the formative moments, the links in the chain — rather than merely stating what a character was. Emphasise development over static portraiture when seeking modern psychological realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealise (universalise) characters by emphasising essential traits
rubrics_metrics.description: To idealise is the representation of an object in its permanent and essential aspects, disengaged from the passing accidents that cling to individuality; the particular is enlarged till it broadens out into the human and the universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit or subordinate transient, local features; throw some commanding quality into relief so the character answers to a 'true idea.' Maintain the equipoise of character so the idealisation does not destroy typical human complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation may also embellish and heighten beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: An idealised representation may seize the object in a happy and characteristic moment, its lines of grace or strength more firmly drawn, its beauty heightened, its significance increased while the likeness to the original is retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select moments and traits that both reveal the type and add aesthetic appeal; idealisation can enhance beauty provided the result remains recognisably human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation does not imply flawless virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s tragic hero is by no means free from faults or failings; some particular quality or group of qualities must be thrown into relief provided the equipoise of character which constitutes a typical human being is not disturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow defects and moral complexity within idealised figures (e.g., Achilles). Avoid flattening characters into morally perfect paragons; the ideal is high but not necessarily perfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy combines the individual with the universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy combines in one harmonious representation the individual and the universal; tragedy manifests the type through the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create rounded characters who are particular people yet exemplify broader human types or truths. Use the individual's fate/actions to illuminate universal ideas; aim for moral and psychological completeness in action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy represents the universal through types rather than historical individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy ... embodies the type rather than the individual, attaching names to characters which are expressive and indicate that the person is not an individual but a type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To generalise in comedy, use character-types and suggestive names to evoke the type immediately. Avoid anchoring comedic action to particular historical personages if you want universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names in comedy should be suggestive/typical
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of adopting historical names poetry gives names of her own invention... The names in that case are expressive; they indicate that the person is not an individual but a type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose names that signal occupation, disposition, or stock role (e.g., 'the Boor', 'the Parasite') to emphasise generalised character. In contrast, historical or highly specific names root characters in particularity and reduce universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: The ludicrous: defect or ugliness that is not painful or destructive
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The ludicrous ... consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive. The comic mask is ugly and distorted, but does not imply pain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for incongruity that is painless — absurdities, blunders, incongruities, disproportion — to provoke laughter without malice or harm. Distinguish this from cruelty, satire, or invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity plus transition produces the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity, in order to be ludicrous, requires a transition, a change of mood, resulting in the discovery either of an unexpected resemblance where there was unlikeness, or of an unexpected unlikeness where there was resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a surprise or shift that reveals incongruity; blend contrasted feelings so the comic effect arises from a painless shock of recognition or contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude malice from the pure ludicrous; avoid mere personal invective
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle omits malice from the definition of the ludicrous; the pleasure of the pure ludicrous is not to be explained by the gratification of malignity. He excludes personal satire and galling caricature from genuine comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your aim is 'pure' comic generalisation, avoid mean-spirited mocking of particular persons; prefer laughter that recognises folly generally rather than humiliates individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's scope: focus on follies and foibles, limit tragic breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: With these defects comedy amuses itself, discovering the inconsistencies which underlie life and character, and exhibiting evil not as it is in its essential nature, but as a thing to be laughed at rather than hated. Comedy ... cannot, while remaining within its own strict limits, present ... a rounded and complete action, an image of universal human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center comedy on lesser, non-fatal human imperfections and ephemeral absurdities; if you need full moral seriousness and complete action, turn to tragedy or hybrid forms (humour with pathos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic characters often embody a single dominant trait
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of character-drawing, its usual method—so far as it maintains itself as a distinct artistic type—is to embody a dominant characteristic or leading passion, so that the single attribute becomes the man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing comedic types, isolate and exaggerate a principal quality to make the type recognisable; beware that excessive one-sidedness runs to caricature and loss of humane depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Comedy: tighter plot and moral probability
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Middle Comedy and still more in the New Comedy ... the action by degrees gains strength and consistency, till, like that of tragedy, it has a beginning, a middle, and an end. Character and action become more intimately united. The typical follies and failings of mankind are woven into a plot in which moral probability takes the place of the arbitrary sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For more sophisticated comedy, integrate character foibles into a coherent, causally plausible plot rather than relying on episodic lampooning; aim for unity of action and believable motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour enriched by sympathy bridges comedy and tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: By the close alliance of sympathy with humour—the most far-reaching results have been produced affecting the range and meaning of the ludicrous. Humour, enriched by sympathy, directs its observation to the more serious realities of life ... It finds everywhere the material both for laughter and tears; and pathos henceforth becomes the companion of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ sympathetic insight in comic writing to deepen effects, allowing humour to reveal tragic or pathos-laden truths; this creates modern comic universality rather than mere ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure realism and pure symbolism in art
rubrics_metrics.description: First, pure realism is forbidden ... Next, pure symbolism is forbidden,—those fantastic shapes ... which were known to the Greeks themselves in the arts of Egypt and Assyria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of slavish, literal imitation that confuses copy with original and of implausible, over-symbolic forms that render ideas as impossible concrete hybrids. Balance representational truth with the requirements of poetic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be selective and critical when applying prescriptive rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's rules are based on a discriminating and selective principle, and imply some criterion for judging of artistic excellence. He does not accept even the greater tragedians as all of equal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rules as generalisations from precedent rather than absolute laws; evaluate works on their merits and historical context, applying Aristotelian precepts discriminatingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of evil and defects is partly a philosophical choice
rubrics_metrics.description: At what precise point imperfections are to be regarded as accidental, abnormal, irregular ... is a problem whose answer will vary at different stages of history, and will admit of different applications according to the particular art that is in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide according to aesthetic and historical context which flaws belong to the 'type' worth representing and which are accidental; be aware that artistic norms change over time and across genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Villains and vicious characters have a restricted dramatic role
rubrics_metrics.description: Even vicious characters are not entirely excluded from tragedy on Aristotle’s theory, though the villain may not hold the position of protagonist. The aesthetic ideal of character in the Poetics implies a high, though not a perfect morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include morally bad characters as part of the dramatic world but avoid making them the central ideal hero; keep the protagonist's moral stature high enough to fulfil tragic requirements without insisting on perfection.
